analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal nationwide to require workers to pay union dues or fees as a job condition.
analysis.headline: The National Right-to-Work Act drew 129 Republican cosponsors but was never taken up by its own committee and died without a House vote when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so that no worker anywhere in the country could be required to join a union or pay union dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job, even in a workplace where a majority of workers voted for union representation. Today, states can ban this under 'right-to-work' laws; about half have. This bill would make that rule national, repealing the sections of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that allow union security agreements. That would cut union funding in every state, including the roughly 25 states that currently allow the fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who object to paying union fees but are covered by a union contract keep more of their paycheck. Unions would still have to represent all workers in a bargaining unit, so nonmembers get the same contract terms for free. Supporters also argue it protects workers from being forced to financially support organizations they disagree with.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who don't want to pay union fees

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the National Labor Relations Act that let employers and unions sign contracts requiring employees to pay dues or fees to keep their job.
Applies the same rule to railroad and airline workers by repealing the Railway Labor Act provisions that permit mandatory dues deduction and union membership requirements.
Would make 'right-to-work' the rule in all 50 states, so a worker's protection would no longer depend on which state they live in.

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions lose the fees and dues from nonmembers they are legally required to represent, shrinking their budgets and bargaining strength. Workers in union shops bear the downstream cost if weaker unions negotiate weaker contracts, since research on state right-to-work laws finds lower wages and fewer union jobs where they apply. Employers gain bargaining leverage from weaker unions.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes unions' main source of steady funding while leaving their legal duty to represent every worker in a bargaining unit intact, which labor economists say shrinks union membership and bargaining power.

Studies of state right-to-work laws consistently find lower wages and lower rates of health and pension coverage in right-to-work states, meaning the individual savings from not paying dues can be outweighed by weaker contracts for everyone.
It lets nonmembers receive the full benefits of a union contract without paying anything toward the cost of negotiating it, which unions call a free-rider problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: An individual worker who dislikes the union can save several hundred to over a thousand dollars a year in fees, and the bill protects sincere freedom of association. But unions would lose billions in revenue nationwide while keeping their duty to represent those same nonpayers, and the track record of state right-to-work laws points to lower average wages for workers, union and nonunion alike. The bill is a genuine trade, and the evidence that the trade nets out badly for workers as a group is what its opponents lean on most.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa, joined by Rep. Joe Wilson of South Carolina, introduced the bill on February 1, 2017.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; no further action of any kind appears in the record.
129 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, and no Democrats did.
The committee held no markup and the House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers whose contracts they defend, who keep union security agreements and the funding that comes with them. Employers and anti-union advocacy groups lose their chance at a national right-to-work law, though right-to-work advocates can try again in a future Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions and workers with union contracts

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on February 1, 2017.

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Joined King in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.name: National Right to Work Committee
for.what_they_did: Longstanding backer of a national right-to-work law; publicly championed the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic caucus
against.what_they_did: No Democrat cosponsored the bill, leaving it with zero support from the party that would have needed to help move it.

against.name: AFL-CIO and organized labor
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against national right-to-work legislation as an existential threat to union funding.

sides.party_line_note: All 129 cosponsors were Republicans and none were Democrats; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call, but the sponsorship lists split cleanly on party lines.

industries.note: The bill repeals the legal basis for union security agreements, cutting unions off from fees and dues from nonmembers they must still represent. Unions' interest here runs with the workers they bargain for, since their funding is what finances contract negotiations, grievance handling, and wage fights.
Weaker unions mean less bargaining pressure over wages, benefits, and work rules. Where state right-to-work laws have been studied, wages tend to be lower — which cuts labor costs for employers.

industries.industry: Nonunion advocacy groups and anti-union legal organizations
industries.note: A national right-to-work law would be the largest expansion of their agenda in decades, shrinking union political spending. Their gain is the mirror image of organized labor's loss, and individual nonmember workers keep their fee money.
